Name: ptcg_agent_evolution
Title: Evolving a Pokémon TCG Battle Agent via Option-Scoring Policy Search in the cabt Simulator
Short Hypothesis: A heuristic option-scoring policy for the Pokémon Trading Card Game — covering lethal-attack detection, energy-attachment planning, bench development, and context-aware card selection — can be systematically improved through iterative search to substantially raise winrate against fixed baseline opponents in the cabt simulator, and card-database-informed lookahead yields further gains over purely reactive scoring.
Related Work: Game-playing agents for imperfect-information card games (Poker CFR lines, Hearthstone/MTG heuristic+search agents, RL for Pokémon TCG Live) typically combine hand-crafted evaluation with search. This task instantiates that program inside the cabt engine (the Kaggle 'pokemon-tcg-ai-battle' competition simulator, shipped with pip kaggle-environments): agents receive an observation with the full visible board state and a list of LEGAL options each decision, and return indices of chosen options. Unlike prior work requiring rules engines to be built, cabt provides perfect legality, so all research effort concentrates on decision quality — scoring, planning, and hidden-information reasoning.
Abstract:
DEPLOYMENT & DEPENDENCY CONSTRAINT (HARD, applies to EVERY candidate, non-negotiable): the option-scoring policy — choose(obs)/agent(obs) and everything they call at decision time — MUST be a self-contained, hand-crafted/rule-based function using ONLY the Python standard library, numpy, and the provided ctypes card DB (AllCard/AllAttack). It is FORBIDDEN to import or use torch, tensorflow, jax, sklearn, or ANY neural-network / gradient-trained / learned-parameter model as the policy, and FORBIDDEN to load weights or any external file at decision time. All improvement MUST come from better hand-crafted evaluation, planning, and lookahead logic — never from a learned function approximator. matplotlib may be used ONLY to render the required experiment figures, never inside the policy. Rationale: the trained agent is deployed into a lightweight Kaggle cabt episode runner with no torch and no persisted state, so any policy depending on torch/NN or saved weights is DISQUALIFIED regardless of winrate (the 2-game smoke test in the eval cascade must import and run the policy with stdlib+numpy only). Keep the final policy a single importable module defining choose(obs)/agent(obs) and the 60-card DECK, and save that exact deployable source as the node's best_solution.

The Pokémon Trading Card Game is a two-player, imperfect-information card game combining resource management (energy attachment), tempo (a race to take 6 prize cards by knocking out opposing Pokémon), and combinatorial card effects. We study policy improvement for a PTCG agent in the cabt simulator available via `from kaggle_environments import make; env = make('cabt')`. Each decision, the engine hands the agent obs['select'] with a list of legal options (typed: main actions PLAY/ATTACH/EVOLVE/ABILITY/ATTACK/RETREAT/END, card picks with area/index, yes-no, counts) plus full visible state in obs['current'] (both players' boards, own hand, prize/deck counts) and obs['logs']; the agent returns a list of option indices (up to maxCount). The first call (obs['select'] is None) must return a fixed legal 60-card deck (provided). We start from a working baseline heuristic (provided in the seed code, ~90% winrate vs the built-in 'random' opponent, ~50% vs the stronger built-in 'first' opponent) and iteratively improve the option-scoring policy, evaluated by winrate over seat-alternated game batches against both baselines. The engine also exposes a complete card/attack database via the provided ctypes bindings (AllCard/AllAttack), enabling effect-aware play and lookahead. The goal is to maximize mean winrate across the two opponents (treated as two evaluation datasets: 'vs_random' and 'vs_first').
Experiments: DEPLOYMENT & DEPENDENCY CONSTRAINT (HARD, applies to EVERY candidate, non-negotiable): the option-scoring policy — choose(obs)/agent(obs) and everything they call at decision time — MUST be a self-contained, hand-crafted/rule-based function using ONLY the Python standard library, numpy, and the provided ctypes card DB (AllCard/AllAttack). It is FORBIDDEN to import or use torch, tensorflow, jax, sklearn, or ANY neural-network / gradient-trained / learned-parameter model as the policy, and FORBIDDEN to load weights or any external file at decision time. All improvement MUST come from better hand-crafted evaluation, planning, and lookahead logic — never from a learned function approximator. matplotlib may be used ONLY to render the required experiment figures, never inside the policy. Rationale: the trained agent is deployed into a lightweight Kaggle cabt episode runner with no torch and no persisted state, so any policy depending on torch/NN or saved weights is DISQUALIFIED regardless of winrate (the 2-game smoke test in the eval cascade must import and run the policy with stdlib+numpy only). Keep the final policy a single importable module defining choose(obs)/agent(obs) and the 60-card DECK, and save that exact deployable source as the node's best_solution. E1 (baseline + evaluation contract): Run the provided seed agent against BOTH built-in opponents 'random' and 'first'. EVALUATION CASCADE (mandatory for every candidate policy): (a) 2-game exception smoke test — any raised exception or non-DONE status disqualifies the candidate; (b) ~20-game screen vs 'first' only — discard candidates clearly below the incumbent; (c) full confirm: 100+ seat-alternated games PER opponent (budget: 400 games costs roughly 2-4 minutes CPU, well within the timeout). STATISTICS: report a 95% Wilson interval for every winrate; a candidate only counts as an improvement if its mean_winrate exceeds the incumbent's with z>=1.6 separation — at N=80 the binomial stderr is ~5.6 percentage points, so small deltas are noise; never promote on noise. RICH DIAGNOSTICS (hard requirement): experiment_data.npy must contain, per opponent: per-seat winrates (seat 0 vs seat 1), win list, cumulative winrate curve, exception/error/timeout counts recorded SEPARATELY (an opponent crash or errored game must never be silently counted as a win), average game length in turns, and 2-3 sentence summaries of up to 5 LOST games extracted from obs['logs'] (what killed us, tempo lost where). Save winrate-curve and final-winrate-bar matplotlib figures. Metric: mean_winrate = (winrate_vs_random + winrate_vs_first)/2, higher is better. SEED HYGIENE: derive all game RNG from the provided `seed` variable; when comparing two policies, evaluate both on the same seed set, and confirm any claimed improvement on a DISJOINT seed set (e.g. seeds 1000+g) before reporting it as the node's result.

E2 (policy improvement increments): Improve the option-scoring policy in measured increments, re-running the E1 cascade after each: (a) lethal-attack detection accounting for weakness (2x damage) and resistance (-30) via the card database; (b) energy-attachment planning toward the exact attack cost ('energies' lists) of the intended attacker instead of always the active Pokemon; (c) bench development: keep 2-3 benched basics as backup attackers and evolve them when possible; (d) context-aware picks: heal the most-damaged own Pokemon, discard the least valuable card, target the opponent Pokemon closest to knockout for damage effects; (e) YES/NO and COUNT decisions tuned per context code. Report the Wilson-bounded winrate delta attributable to each increment; explicitly mark increments whose delta is within noise. DIVERSITY: when drafting multiple independent implementations, condition each on a DISTINCT playstyle archetype (aggressive tempo race / bench-development engine / defensive lookahead trading) rather than three variations of the same idea — vs_random is near ceiling (~90%) for any sane policy, so real signal lives in vs_first and in HOW games are won.

E3 (lookahead and card-effect awareness): Use the provided AllCard/AllAttack ctypes card database to (a) rank attacks by expected effective damage including weakness/resistance, and (b) implement a 1-ply lookahead that checks whether the opponent's active Pokemon can knock out our attacker next turn (from its visible attacks and attached energy), preferring lines that take a prize without giving one back. Compare vs the best E2 policy with the full E1 cascade and Wilson-bounded deltas.

E4 (ablation + final selection): Starting from the best policy found, disable one component at a time (lethal detection, energy planning, bench development, lookahead) and measure the Wilson-bounded winrate drop on both opponents. FINAL SELECTION: re-evaluate the top 2-3 candidate policies on a FRESH, never-before-used seed set with at least 250 games per opponent, and report a regression matrix (per-opponent x per-seat winrates with intervals) — the final reported best policy is chosen by this held-out confirmation, not by the search-time scores.
Risk Factors and Limitations: DEPLOYABILITY DRIFT: prior runs saw the coder add a torch nn.Module OptionScorer whose weights were never saved — undeployable AND unverifiable. The HARD deployment constraint above forbids this; every node must keep the policy stdlib+numpy only and save the deployable source.

NOISE-CLIMBING is the primary failure mode: at 80 games binomial stderr is ~5.6pp, so greedy selection between candidates within a few points of each other is a coin flip; all improvement claims must be Wilson-bounded (z>=1.6) and confirmed on disjoint seeds, else the search performs a random walk that looks like progress.

vs_random is near ceiling (~90%) for any competent policy, so movement in mean_winrate is dominated by vs_first plus noise; per-opponent and per-seat breakdowns must be inspected, never the aggregate alone.

The built-in 'random' and 'first' opponents are weak scripted baselines; winrate against them may overestimate strength against diverse ladder opponents on Kaggle (Goodhart risk). Diagnostics that explain HOW games are won (tempo, prize race speed, comeback rate) partially mitigate this.
Errored, crashed, or timed-out games must be recorded separately and never counted as wins — scoring an opponent crash as a policy win is a classic evaluator exploit.
Each evaluation game costs roughly 0.3-0.6 seconds CPU; the evaluation cascade must stay well within the execution timeout, bounding candidates measurable per node.
The agent must NEVER raise an exception during a game (an exception forfeits the game); all policy code must be wrapped with a safe fallback returning the first maxCount legal option indices.
Hidden information (opponent hand, prize contents, deck order) is invisible; only opponent board, counts, and logs are available, limiting lookahead accuracy.
